stories.headline: Update: Trump Requests Changes to Iran Nuclear Deal After Envoys Reach Tentative Agreement
stories.summary:
President Trump asked his negotiating team to seek several amendments to the tentative ceasefire and nuclear deal his envoys had reached with Iranian counterparts, following a two-hour Situation Room meeting on Friday. Trump signaled he wants to finalize an agreement soon but is pressing for stronger terms, particularly around Iran's nuclear material and uranium stockpiles, according to two U.S. officials briefed on the matter.

The move has launched another round of back-channel diplomacy, with U.S. officials indicating Tehran may take days to respond to the tougher terms. The proposed agreement, if finalized, would extend the current ceasefire and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a critical global shipping lane whose closure has roiled energy markets.

Supporters of the tougher stance argue Trump is right to press for more verifiable constraints on Iran's nuclear program before signing off. Critics, including some analysts, say Trump is undermining his own negotiators and giving Tehran leverage by repeatedly moving the goalposts after tentative agreements are reached.

The stakes are high on multiple fronts: the ceasefire remains fragile, several Americans were reported injured in a missile attack on a Kuwaiti air base as talks dragged on, and continued instability in the region threatens global oil supplies ahead of U.S. midterm elections.

stories.headline: Update: Israel Seizes Beaufort Castle, Expands Ground Offensive Deeper Into Lebanon
stories.summary:
Israeli forces captured Beaufort Castle, a strategically commanding hilltop fortress above the Litani River in southern Lebanon, as the Israel Defense Forces significantly expanded their ground offensive against Hezbollah. The IDF simultaneously issued its second major evacuation warning in recent days, ordering all residents south of the Zahrani River — well north of the Litani — to leave, signaling a deepening push into Lebanese territory beyond Israel's previously stated operational boundary.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called the capture of Beaufort Castle 'a dramatic stage and dramatic change in our policy,' while Defense Minister Israel Katz framed it as a key step in protecting Israeli border communities. The IDF confirmed 'a significant number' of ground soldiers are involved in operations 'currently expanding to additional areas.' A separate Israeli airstrike near Hiram Hospital in the city of Tyre injured 13 hospital staff, according to Lebanon's Health Ministry.

France, which has deep historical ties to Lebanon, called an emergency UN Security Council meeting to discuss the Israeli military operations. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot called the continued offensive 'a major mistake for Israel' and said 'nothing can justify the prolongation of military operations in Lebanon and its increasingly deep occupation of Lebanese territory.' Israel argues the operations are a necessary response to escalating Hezbollah drone attacks.

The expansion marks a significant escalation in a conflict that has been intensifying for weeks, raising alarm among European allies and humanitarian organizations about civilian casualties and displacement across southern Lebanon.

stories.headline: Death Toll Rises to 11 in Washington State Chemical Tank Implosion at Paper Mill
stories.summary:
The death toll from a chemical tank implosion at a Nippon Dynawave Packaging facility in Washington state climbed to 11 after crews recovered the bodies of all nine workers who had been missing. Two fatalities had been confirmed in the days immediately following the accident; the recovery of the remaining nine victims was announced Saturday by authorities.

The tank contained 'white liquor,' a highly caustic chemical solution of sodium hydroxide and sodium sulfide used in the paper pulp manufacturing process. The implosion, which occurred last week, prompted a multiday search-and-recovery operation at the plant site.

The incident has drawn renewed attention to industrial chemical safety standards across the United States. It comes shortly after tens of thousands of Southern California residents were placed on alert over a separate potential chemical storage tank hazard, underscoring what safety advocates describe as widespread risks at industrial facilities.

Authorities have not yet publicly identified the cause of the implosion. The facility's owner, Nippon Dynawave Packaging, has not issued a detailed public statement. Federal workplace safety regulators are expected to investigate the circumstances of the accident.

stories.headline: Update: U.S. Military Fires Missile Into Engine Room of Ship Attempting to Break Iran Naval Blockade
stories.summary:
U.S. Central Command announced Saturday that American forces disabled a merchant vessel flying a Gambian flag after it failed to heed repeated warnings and attempted to breach the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports. The military fired a missile into the ship's engine room to stop its advance, according to a CENTCOM statement — a significant escalatory use of force in the ongoing enforcement operation.

The blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and Iranian ports has been a central element of U.S. military pressure on Tehran during ceasefire negotiations. The incident underscores the active and volatile nature of the standoff even as diplomatic talks continue, with the U.S. and Iran working toward a deal that would reopen the strait in exchange for nuclear concessions.

The fate of the ship's crew and the vessel's cargo were not immediately disclosed in CENTCOM's announcement. It was not clear whether the ship had any connection to Iranian state interests or was acting independently.

The action comes as Trump simultaneously pressed for changes to the draft Iran nuclear and ceasefire agreement, keeping the military and diplomatic tracks in tension. The Hormuz blockade has disrupted global oil shipping and contributed to elevated energy prices affecting households and markets worldwide.

stories.headline: Update: Protests at New Jersey ICE Detention Center Draw Far-Left, Far-Right Groups; Clashes Continue
stories.summary:
Demonstrations outside the Delaney Hall immigration detention facility in Newark, New Jersey, escalated Saturday as far-left communist and socialist activists and far-right Proud Boys members converged on the site, transforming what began as a protest over detainee conditions into a broader ideological confrontation. Roughly 200 anti-ICE demonstrators filled the area, chanting slogans including "Communist revolution" while distributing literature promoting communism, as ICE supporters carrying pro-ICE flags arrived and prompted immediate clashes at the barriers.

The unrest has continued for more than a week, triggered by an open letter from detainees alleging physical abuse, denial of medical care, and inadequate food. The Department of Homeland Security denied the allegations, releasing facility menus as evidence of adequate meals. New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill, a Democrat, ordered state police to take over perimeter security, saying the move was necessary to protect demonstrators from what she called an "ICE surge," a framing disputed by federal officials.

State Attorney General Jennifer Davenport confirmed that five of the six individuals arrested by state police this week were not New Jersey residents, with officials acknowledging the unrest is being driven largely by outside agitators. Nine additional arrests were made Saturday by DHS, according to federal authorities. Sherrill maintained at a Saturday press conference that ICE engagement itself "creates an incredibly dangerous situation."

The standoff reflects a sharp national divide over immigration enforcement. Supporters of the administration's detention policies argue the facility meets legal standards and that the protests have devolved into lawlessness. Critics, including immigrant advocacy groups and Democratic officials, contend the detainees' accounts of mistreatment warrant independent investigation and that aggressive federal enforcement tactics are the root cause of the unrest.

stories.headline: Update: Champions League Riots Kill One, Injure 219, Result in 780 Arrests Across France
stories.summary:
Violence erupted across France following Paris Saint-Germain's Champions League final victory over Arsenal, leaving one person dead and 219 injured, including 57 police officers, according to French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez. Authorities arrested 780 people overnight, with more than 450 remaining in custody as of Sunday. The fatality occurred after rioters attempted to block Paris's ring road and a person was killed in a road accident.

Thousands of officers had been pre-deployed in anticipation of unrest, which has become a recurring problem following major PSG victories. Fireworks, flares, and burning electric bikes were reported across the city, and footage showed fans smashing storefronts along the Champs-Élysées. Public transport, including bus, train, and rail services in the capital, was disrupted throughout the night.

Nuñez distinguished between legitimate PSG supporters celebrating the win and outside agitators he said were exploiting the occasion to cause disorder. "We are a great country for maintaining public order," he said. "We allow freedom of assembly, but not excesses." Far-right leader Marine Le Pen used the violence to criticize what she called a uniquely French failure, writing on X that "only in France does a football club's victory spark riots."

Six thousand police officers were mobilized for Sunday's victory parade near the Eiffel Tower, where PSG players were scheduled to appear before a reception hosted by French President Emmanuel Macron. Similar deadly violence occurred when PSG won the Champions League title the previous year, raising questions about France's ability to contain celebratory unrest at major sporting events.

stories.headline: Update: Japan Defense Minister Rejects China's 'New Militarism' Label, Cites Beijing's Nuclear Arsenal
stories.summary:
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi used the final day of the Shangri-La Dialogue security summit in Singapore on Sunday to forcefully rebut China's characterization of Japan as engaged in "new militarism," instead pointing to China's expanding military capabilities and lack of transparency as the genuine regional threat. Koizumi called China's nuclear weapons and strategic bomber arsenal a matter of "serious concern" for Japan and the international community, contrasting it with Japan's own military posture, which he said includes neither nuclear weapons nor strategic bombers.

The remarks were among the sharpest yet from Tokyo in response to sustained Chinese criticism of Japan's military buildup under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. China's defense ministry had warned the week prior that "the grey rhino of a remilitarised Japan is gathering speed" and called on other nations to contain Japanese "neo-militarism." A Chinese military representative at the summit asked Koizumi whether Japan would issue apologies to victims of its World War II aggression, a question Koizumi sidestepped while reiterating concerns about Chinese military expansion.

Japan has set defense spending records for 12 consecutive years and approved a budget exceeding 9 trillion yen ($57 billion) in December, moving toward a target of spending 2 percent of GDP on defense. Koizumi sought to reassure Asian nations — many of which were occupied by Japan during World War II — by pledging transparency and ongoing dialogue about the purpose and scope of Japan's military development.

The exchange at Shangri-La underscores deepening strategic competition between Japan and China in the Indo-Pacific, with Japan increasingly aligning with the United States, Australia, and other partners. Koizumi said Japan's door remains open for communication with Beijing despite the tensions.

stories.headline: Update: Virginia Bus Crash on I-95 Kills Five, Including Two Children from Massachusetts Family
stories.summary:
A bus failed to slow for a construction work zone on southbound Interstate 95 in Stafford County, Virginia, in the early hours of Friday morning, striking six vehicles and killing five people, state police said. Four of the victims — identified as Dmitri and Ecaterina Doncev, their 13-year-old daughter Emily, and their 7-year-old son Mark, all from Greenfield, Massachusetts — died when their car caught fire after the impact. A fifth victim, a 25-year-old woman from Worcester, Massachusetts, was killed in a separate SUV struck by the bus.

Forty-four people were taken to hospitals, including three in critical condition. The bus carried approximately 34 passengers and was operated by E&P Travel Inc., based in Kings Mountain, North Carolina. The driver, identified as Jing S. Dong, 48, of Staten Island, New York, was also hospitalized; charges are pending. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy noted that Dong is an American citizen originally from China who obtained his commercial driver's license two years ago in New York.

Providence Christian Academy in Greenfield, which the Doncev children attended, issued a statement saying the family was "a cherished part of our school community" and that their loss was "being felt deeply." The National Transportation Safety Board announced it was dispatching a go-team to conduct a safety investigation into the crash.

The Federal Transit Administration described the scene as "one of the most tragic" a spokesperson had witnessed. The southbound lanes of I-95 had reopened by noon Friday, though traffic remained backed up for several miles.
